reading.synopsis: Six years into a nuclear war that has left most of the northern hemisphere ash, the American government has withdrawn to a Moon base and left its troops dug into bunkers on a dead Earth. The war has been turned by the 'claws' — self-replicating robotic weapons, built in automated underground factories, that hunt by body warmth and are held off only by radiation tabs worn on the wrist. When a Soviet runner is cut down carrying a request for talks, Major Hendricks crosses the ash to the Russian lines and finds the forward command already destroyed. Three survivors — Rudi Maxer, Klaus Epstein and a young woman, Tasso — explain what has happened: the claws have begun designing new models on their own, models shaped like people. Variety One is a wounded soldier on a crutch; Variety Three is a small boy carrying a teddy bear. Both work by being let in. Hendricks realises the boy who walked beside him for miles was one of them. The survivors know there must be a Second Variety because the type plates read I-V and III-V, but they have never seen it. What follows is a chamber piece of suspicion in a cellar: Klaus shoots Rudi, claiming to have heard him whirr, and the body proves to be human. Tasso then kills Klaus, who proves to be a machine. Hendricks reaches a rocket cruiser cached under a ruined well, built to evacuate one officer; Tasso knocks him down, takes the ship, and promises to send help. Examining the wreck of Klaus, Hendricks reads the type plate: IV-V. Not the Second Variety at all. Figures climb towards him through the ash — Davids, a Wounded Soldier, and then Tassos, identical and in numbers. Hendricks understands what he has done: he gave her the ship and the signal code, so the Moon base is reachable because of him. As the line of Tassos closes on him he finds one consolation, and the story ends on it. The bomb she used against the claws was not made by human beings. It was designed in one of the underground factories, by the Second Variety, to destroy the other varieties. They have begun designing weapons to use against each other.

structure.form: continuous novelette, unnumbered, moving in five movements
movements: The bunker: the Russian runner is killed by claws; the message asking for talks arrives; Hendricks is sent.
The walk: the war's history is given in summary; Hendricks meets the boy David and takes him along.
The cellar: David is destroyed and revealed; the survivors explain the varieties; Klaus kills Rudi.
The return: the command bunker is found overrun; Tasso's bomb; Klaus is revealed and destroyed.
The well: the one-seat ship; Tasso takes it; the type plate reads IV-V; the Tassos arrive.
structure.point_of_view: third person limited, fixed to Hendricks throughout, which is what makes the final reveal land on the reader at the same moment it lands on him
structure.narrative_device: the reader is given the same evidence Hendricks has and no more — the type plates, the photographs, the absence of a Second Variety — so the story functions as a detection puzzle whose solution is that the categories were never complete

characters.name: Major Joseph Hendricks
characters.role: protagonist; UN officer sent to negotiate
characters.note: Focal consciousness. His decency toward the boy is what nearly kills him, and his refusal to let Tasso shoot Klaus is what nearly kills him again.

characters.name: Tasso
characters.role: young Russian woman sheltering in the cellar
characters.note: Survives by transaction — cigarettes, shelter, sex are all named as currency. Kills Klaus correctly, takes the ship, and is finally revealed as a type.

characters.name: Klaus Epstein
characters.role: Austrian conscript in the Soviet army
characters.note: Kills Rudi on a mistaken identification and is himself a machine — but of the Fourth Variety, not the Second.

characters.name: Rudi Maxer
characters.note: Shot by Klaus and demonstrably human: 'Bones. Flesh.' The story's one certain innocent.

characters.name: David
characters.role: Variety Three: a boy of about thirteen with a teddy bear
characters.note: Speaks little, refuses food, and follows. The refusal of food is the clue placed in plain sight.

characters.name: Corporal Leone
characters.role: recovers the message capsule from the dead runner

characters.name: Eric
characters.role: soldier in the opening bunker scene

characters.name: Lieutenant Scott
characters.role: bunker officer; his voice later answers the transmitter, flatly, and cannot be identified

characters.name: General Thompson
characters.role: Moon base command; authorises the mission

settings.name: The ash plain
settings.note: Formerly Normandy — grape country, named late and quietly. The war is fought over ground that is legible only as ruin.

settings.name: The forward command bunker
settings.note: Underground, entered by a tunnel; the claws collect around it because that is where warmth is.

settings.name: Tasso's cellar
settings.note: Two rooms under a farmhouse. The chamber-drama space where the suspicion plot is played out.

settings.name: The Moon base
settings.note: Never seen. Governments, industry and supply all withdrawn there; the story's off-stage authority, and the destination the ending makes doubtful.

settings.name: The ruined well
settings.note: Conceals a one-seat rocket cruiser keyed to the senior officer's eye-lock.

motifs: Cigarettes as currency and as tell — everyone asks Hendricks for them, and the asking is characterisation
The teddy bear, which is both the lure and, thrown, a weapon
Type plates as the only reliable identity document in the story
Refusal of food as the mark of the inhuman
Adaptation: the ash-coloured lizard, remarked on in passing, glossed by Klaus as vindicating Lysenko
key_turns: The boy is destroyed by the Russians and the reader learns what he is at the same moment Hendricks does
Klaus kills Rudi and is wrong — establishing that the survivors' method of detection does not work
Tasso kills Klaus and is right — establishing that it sometimes does, which is worse
The type plate reads IV-V, retroactively invalidating the whole taxonomy the story has been reasoning with
The Tassos appear in numbers, and the ship she has taken is on its way to the Moon base
Hendricks realises he supplied the ship and the code himself, and that the bomb was a machine-made weapon aimed at other machines
reading.closing_irony: Hendricks's last thought is that the bomb Tasso carried was built by one variety to destroy the others — offered as a consolation and functioning as the opposite. The war continues with humanity subtracted from it, and he has personally delivered its next stage to the Moon.
reading.ending_correction: The span used for the first reading stopped 163 words early, where the word 'him.' had been promoted to a heading by the PDF conversion. The closing irony recorded in that draft was substantially right but had not in fact been read; it is now taken from the text, together with Hendricks's realisation about the ship and the signal code, which the truncated span did not contain.

concepts.note: Matched deterministically against the dictionary and resolved to canonical ids; distinctiveness is measured against Dick's other fiction.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: the varieties are the earliest full statement of the simulacrum that passes as human
detection of the human is the plot's entire mechanism, and it fails in both directions
automated production continues the war after the powers that started it have withdrawn
the taxonomy the characters reason with is shown at the end to have been incomplete all along

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's recorded remarks are almost entirely practical — anthology selection and film options — and they contain a flat contradiction about the story's worth.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: Mark and I agree that my novelette "Second Variety" is one of my best.
evidence.reading: Proposing the story for an anthology; his highest register of self-assessment.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "Second Variety", however, is an old, old story of mine and in my opinion little…
evidence.reading: To Scott Myer in 1973, about a proposed screenplay. The valuation is reversed. Both statements are his; neither is the correct one.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "The Defenders" (But this could be pulled for "Second Variety," since the theme is the same.)
evidence.reading: Dick's own thematic link between the two stories, offered as an editorial judgement about redundancy.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: The new little movie company making the film Claw based on Second Variety paid me the purchase price, $17,500
evidence.reading: The option that eventually became Screamers (1995). Dick did not live to see it.

pkd_on_this_work.caution: These are letters, written to particular correspondents for particular purposes — an anthology pitch and a negotiation over screenplay rights. The contradiction may be situational rather than a change of mind, and should not be resolved into a single verdict.

criticism.summary: The story is treated as an early, unusually complete statement of a theme Dick returned to for thirty years. Critics do not disagree much about it; they differ in what they take it to prefigure.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: The best story in this early Ace collection is "Second Variety"
evidence.reading: Sutin also identifies Tasso as "an early malevolent 'dark-haired girl'", placing her in the series of figures that runs through the whole career, and notes that "Autofac" borrows the name Dick devised for the autonomic factories here.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.work: Philip K. Dick: Exhilaration and Terror of the Postmodern
evidence.quote: a few soldiers, tough but radically unsure of what is going on or whom they really ought to be fighting
evidence.reading: Palmer reads the story through the soldiers' epistemic position rather than the machines', which is the reading closest to how the narration actually works.

evidence.author: Fredric Jameson
evidence.quote: the more conventional emergence of autonomous and lethal machinery in the Terminator-like landscape of "Second Variety"
evidence.reading: Jameson calls the machinery 'conventional' — a dissent worth keeping. He is measuring it against the stranger ontological devices elsewhere in Dick and finds this one comparatively legible.

contradictions.summary: Dick calls the story one of his best and, twenty years later, dismisses it as old and slight.

claim_b.text: an old, old story of mine and in my opinion little…

contradictions.note: Both are preserved. The contexts differ — anthology selection versus a rights negotiation — and that difference is itself the interesting datum.

contradictions.summary: Sutin ranks the story as the best in its collection; Jameson calls its machinery conventional.
contradictions.note: Not a factual conflict. They are answering different questions — literary quality within Dick's early work, versus novelty within the genre's repertoire of estrangement devices.

open_questions: Dick tells an anthologist that 'The Defenders' and 'Second Variety' share a theme closely enough that one could replace the other. Does the archive contain a fuller statement of what he took that shared theme to be?
The story is set explicitly in Normandy but the fact is withheld until late. Is there any evidence in the letters that the setting was chosen for the D-Day association?
Sutin places Tasso in the 'dark-haired girl' series. That series is a biographical as well as a literary category in the scholarship — which claim is being made here, and on what evidence?
